property_summary: For any oracleVersion id, C.atVersion(oracleVersion) always returns an OracleVersion whose price equals the payoffDefinition-transformed oracle().atVersion(...) price (i.e. transformed price), whereas the mutant returns the raw oracle price for some oracleVersion, so the returned price can differ.

For every oracleVersion id, C.atVersion(id) returns an OracleVersion whose price equals the payoffDefinition-transformed oracle().atVersion(id).price; the mutant returns the raw oracle price for some id, so prices can differ.

For every oracleVersion id, C.atVersion(id) returns an OracleVersion whose price equals the payoffDefinition-transformed oracle().atVersion(id).price; the mutant returns the raw oracle price for some id, so there exists an id where returned.price differs.

For every oracleVersion id, calling atVersion(id) on the product returns an OracleVersion whose price equals the product's payoffDefinition.transform applied to the underlying oracle().atVersion(id).price; the mutant (which forwards oracle().atVersion without transforming) will for some oracleVersion return a price that differs.

For every oracleVersion id, C.atVersion(id) returns an OracleVersion whose price equals the payoffDefinition-transformed price of the underlying oracle().atVersion(id); the mutant forwards oracle().atVersion(id) without transforming, so for some oracleVersion the returned price will differ.

For any account address, the correct contract returns the stored per-account maintenance() (which may be non-zero) while the mutant returns ZERO for all accounts; therefore there exists some account for which maintenance(account) != 0 and the mutant will differ (the test fuzzes an account and asserts maintenance(account) == 0 only in the mutant, so the reference preserves the stored value and the mutant fails for accounts with non-zero maintenance).

For every account, the deployed reference contract returns the account-specific stored maintenance() value (whatever it is), whereas the mutant always returns ZERO for every account—so there exist accounts for which maintenance(account) != ZERO and the mutant breaks the rule.

For any account, the reference contract returns whatever per-account maintenance() getter reports (possibly non-zero) while the mutant always returns ZERO; therefore there exists an account for which maintenance(account) != ZERO and the mutant breaks the equality between stored maintenance and a non-zero result — we assert that maintenance(account) is not always ZERO by fuzzing accounts and requiring the returned value equals the stored getter call (i.e. is allowed to be non-zero) — the mutant will fail for accounts whose stored maintenance is non-zero.

For any account address, the real contract's maintenance(account) call returns whatever the contract's per-account maintenance getter reports (which can be non-zero for some accounts); the mutant always returns ZERO, so there exist fuzzed accounts for which maintenance(account) != 0 and thus the mutant violates the property.

For every account address, calling maintenance(account) on the correct contract returns whatever the contract's stored per-account maintenance getter (maintenance) returns (which can be non-zero for some accounts); the mutant always returns ZERO breaking this rule for accounts whose stored maintenance is non-zero.

For any contract state, takerFee() returns exactly the stored _takerFee; the mutant that multiplies the stored value by 2 will cause takerFee() to return a value equal to 2 * stored value for some stored values, violating equality with the stored value.

For every stored taker fee value in the contract, calling takerFee() returns that stored UFixed18 value (i.e. the getter reflects storage); the mutant that multiplies the stored value by 2 will produce a different returned UFixed18 for some stored values, violating this storage-reflection property.

For any stored taker fee value, calling takerFee() returns a UFixed18 whose unwrap equals the exact stored _takerFee value (the correct contract returns storage as-is; the mutant that multiplies by 2 will violate this for some stored values).

For any stored taker fee value, calling takerFee() produces a UFixed18 whose unwrap is less-than-or-equal-to the maximum uint256 (always true) and, specifically, the reference returns a value equal to the stored _takerFee while the mutant sometimes returns double that stored value; we assert equality between takerFee() and calling updateTakerFee then reading takerFee() after storing the same value via the public update path (fuzzer chooses the fee) — the reference preserves the written value, the mutant (which doubles on read) will break for many non-zero inputs.

For any UFixed18 value written via updateTakerFee, calling takerFee() returns exactly that stored UFixed18 value; the mutant that returns double the stored value will cause takerFee() to differ for some fuzzed inputs.

For any deployed product contract C, its public getter positionFee() returns the stored position fee value (positionFee storage) equal to the product's configured position fee; the mutant that returns makerFee() will sometimes return a different value when makerFee != positionFee, violating this equality.
For any configured product, positionFee() must return the stored position fee value; the mutant returning makerFee() violates this whenever makerFee != positionFee.

For any product initialization inputs, the public getter positionFee() returns the positionFee value supplied at initialization; the mutant returning makerFee() violates this whenever the initialized makerFee != positionFee (the fuzzer will find such inputs).

For every initialization of C, the public getter positionFee() returns the positionFee value stored in storage (the initialized positionFee); the mutant that returns makerFee() will produce a different return for some initializations where makerFee != positionFee.

For any initialization inputs, the public getter positionFee() must return the product's configured positionFee (the stored position fee); the mutant that reads makerFee instead will return a different value whenever the initialized makerFee != positionFee, so there exist fuzzed inputs (makerFee != positionFee) that make the mutant fail.

For any newMaintenance value, calling updateMaintenance(newMaintenance) stores the same value in the product's maintenance() getter (reference C always writes _maintenance via helper _updateMaintenance); the mutant that bypasses the helper can be distinguished because _productVersion() used in the emitted event (and possibly other side-effects) differs when called during settleProduct — the safe rule is that after updateMaintenance returns, maintenance() equals the supplied newMaintenance for all inputs; the mutant can violate this by storing to a different slot/ordering causing maintenance() to not match the supplied value for some inputs.

For any caller who is the product owner, calling updateMaintenance(newMaintenance) results in maintenance() returning exactly newMaintenance (reference preserves this for all inputs; the mutant that bypasses the helper can fail to store/read the same value for some inputs).

For any arbitrary UFixed18 value provided by a product owner, after calling updateMaintenance(newMaintenance) the contract's maintenance() getter must equal the supplied newMaintenance; the mutant that stores directly to the storage slot (bypassing the helper) can cause maintenance() to differ for some inputs.

For any caller who is the product owner and any UFixed18 value, calling updateMaintenance(newMaintenance) must result in maintenance() returning exactly the supplied newMaintenance; the mutant that writes directly to storage (bypassing the helper) can cause maintenance() to differ for some inputs and thus violate this invariant.
